title: Easing, past Easy Ease
blurb: Why the default curve makes everything feel the same, and how to leave it.

text.v: Easy Ease is a fine curve. The problem is that it is the same curve every time, on every property, in every piece, and after a while your work has one accent.
What a curve is actually saying

A curve is a claim about weight. A move that starts slowly and arrives quickly reads as something falling. One that leaves fast and settles slowly reads as something thrown. Easy Ease sits politely in the middle and says very little.
The fastest way to hear the difference is to keep a move identical and change only its curve.

blocks.caption: Same distance, same duration. The curve is doing all the talking.

text.v: Two numbers, and that is most of it
Open the graph editor. You are looking at two handles.

items.v: How long the move holds back before it commits.
Drag the first handle right and the thing hesitates.
How long it takes to settle at the end.
Drag the second handle left and it lands hard, right and it glides in.

text.v: Almost everything you like in other people's work is one of those two pushed further than feels comfortable.
Overshoot is not a third thing. It is the second handle taken past the value and allowed to come back. If it feels like a separate trick, you have not pushed the settle far enough yet.
The exercise that fixes this fastest

Take one move you already made. Duplicate it three times, side by side. Give the first a hard landing, the second a long settle, the third a hesitation before it leaves. Same distance, same duration. Watch all three loop together.
You will pick a favourite within a minute, and it will not be the middle one.
Once a single move has a curve you chose, the next question is what happens when there are five of them, and whether they should share it. That is spacing, and it is the next piece.
